facts.claim: Walker's lab found overnight motor-skill gains tied to stage 2 NREM sleep spindles, especially in the last two hours of an eight-hour night (e.g. 5 to 7 a.m. if asleep at 11 p.m.) - the hours many cut short.
Walker pictures the Olympic coach who trains athletes late and wakes them early, denying that late-night phase.
Usain Bolt has on many occasions napped in the hours before breaking the world record and before Olympic finals he won.

Walker tells sports teams that sleep is a powerful, legal performance enhancer; with less than eight and especially less than six hours, time to physical exhaustion drops 10 to 30 percent and aerobic output falls.
A 2014 study of competitive young athletes (Milewski et al.) found chronic short sleep across a season predicted much higher injury risk.

Walker shows teams sleep-tracker data from Andre Iguodala (Golden State Warriors): with more than eight hours vs less, +12% minutes played, +29% points per minute, +2% three-point percentage, +9% free-throw percentage; with less sleep +37% turnovers and +45% fouls.

Residents on a thirty-hour straight shift commit 36% more serious medical errors (wrong drug dose, surgical implement left inside) than those working sixteen hours or less, and after such a shift make 460% more diagnostic mistakes in the ICU.
facts.source: archive.org full text; Landrigan NEJM 2004 via search

facts.claim: After a thirty-hour shift residents are 73% more likely to stab themselves with a needle or cut themselves with a scalpel, and 168% more likely to have a car crash driving home.
An attending surgeon not allowed at least a six-hour sleep opportunity the night before has a 170% increased risk of a serious surgical error such as organ damage or major haemorrhage.

An Australian study: after nineteen hours awake, sleep-deprived people were as cognitively impaired as those at the legal driving limit (0.08% blood alcohol); the decline began after fifteen hours awake. Walker asks whether you would accept treatment from a doctor who took swigs from a hip flask.

In Dinges's study, ten days of six hours of sleep a night made people as impaired as 24 hours without sleep; participants consistently underestimated their impairment, 'like someone at a bar ... telling you I'm fine to drive home'.
Pilot studies limiting residents to sixteen-hour shifts with an eight-hour rest cut serious medical errors by over 20%.

Chapter 10 'Dreaming as Overnight Therapy': Walker tested whether time heals all wounds or time spent in dream sleep. During REM sleep, noradrenaline is completely shut off in the brain - the only time in 24 hours - while emotion and memory regions (amygdala, hippocampus) reactivate.

Experiment: healthy young adults viewed emotional images in an MRI scanner twice, twelve hours apart; half saw them morning then evening (awake), half evening then next morning (after sleep). Those who slept felt significantly less emotional and showed a large drop in amygdala reactivity with prefrontal re-engagement; the awake group did not. REM sleep quality predicted the effect.
Walker's phrase: REM sleep is 'sleeping to remember' the details and 'sleeping to forget' the painful emotional charge.

Dr. Murray Raskind at a VA hospital near Seattle gave veterans with PTSD the blood-pressure drug prazosin; their recurring nightmares eased. Prazosin suppresses noradrenaline in the brain, matching Walker's theory.
Caveat: a large 2018 VA trial (Raskind et al., NEJM) found prazosin did not reduce trauma nightmares more than placebo in chronic PTSD veterans.
Caveat: Why We Sleep has been criticised for overstating some figures (e.g. Guzey's review).

Post-game sleep speeds recovery from inflammation, stimulates muscle repair and restocks glucose and glycogen; IOC 2015 consensus statement on sleep in athletic development; small margins separate gold from last.
Baseline resetting: with chronic sleep restriction people acclimate to impaired performance as their normal. Irony: a resident leaving the ER may return as a crash victim after a microsleep.
